name: Existence of dharmas in the three times (sarvāstivāda)

definitions.definition: Dharmas of past, present and future all exist as real entities; proven by scripture, by consciousness arising from two, by consciousness requiring an existent object, and by the results of past karma; the times differ only by activity.
Only the present exists; the conditioned arises having not been and ceases having been; results come from the transformed series.
Only unripened past karma exists of the past (Vibhajyavāda position).
Past and future do not exist as entities (Vasumitra).
Rejected in Kathāvatthu 1.6–1.8.

relations.note: The Sautrāntika alternative rests on momentariness.

name: The four masters on existence in the three times

definitions.definition: Dharmatrāta: change of mode of being (bhāva); Ghoṣaka: of characteristic (lakṣaṇa); Vasumitra: of state (avasthā); Buddhadeva: of relation (anyathānyathika). Vasumitra's is best — the times are fixed by activity.

name: The seventy-five dharmas in five groups

definitions.definition: The later Vaibhāṣika count of the real dharmas: 11 of matter, 1 mind, 46 mental factors, 14 dissociated formations, 3 unconditioned — built from the Kośa's classification.
The Prakaraṇapāda's fivefold division (matter, mind, mental factors, dissociated, unconditioned) is the basis of the list.

notes: The number 75 is a later (East Asian / Tibetan scholastic) count from the Kośa; the Kośa itself does not state the total.

name: The mental factors in six classes

definitions.definition: Ten universal, ten universal good, six universal defiled, two universal bad, ten restricted defiled, and (in the later count) eight undetermined (remorse, sleepiness, reasoning, investigation, passion, aversion, pride, doubt).

Real forces neither material nor mental: possession, non-possession, homogeneity, the non-perceptual state, the two attainments, life faculty, the four characteristics, and the three collections of names, phrases, syllables.
Designations for states of the series.
A real force that links a dharma to a series; explains ownership of latent defilements and of attainments.
The intact seed in the series; not an entity.

relations.note: The two explanations of the same function.

name: The four characteristics of the conditioned

definitions.definition: Birth, duration, decay and impermanence as real forces, with secondary characteristics.
Designations of the series: arising having not been, ceasing having been, the continuity and its change.
Space, cessation through discernment, cessation not through discernment — real and eternal.
Not entities: mere absences.
Nine unconditioned (Vasumitra; low confidence).
Nine unconditioned (Vasumitra; low confidence).
A good or bad material continuum produced by action or concentration, carrying vows and non-vows.
Unreal; the continuity of karma is the transformed series.

name: Six causes, four conditions, five results

definitions.definition: Six causes (efficient, co-existent, homogeneous, associated, pervasive, ripening), four conditions (causal, immediately preceding, object, dominant), five results (ripening, outflow, dominant, human effort, disjunction); nothing arises from a single cause such as Īśvara.
Faculties by dominance: six sense, female, male, life, five feelings, five spiritual, three pure.

name: Conventional and ultimate existence in the Kośa

definitions.definition: What loses its identity when broken or analysed (pot, water) exists conventionally; what does not (matter, feeling) exists ultimately.
Expressions like 'the eye sees' are conventions used at will over a mere flow of dharmas.
Destruction needs no cause; everything arisen perishes of itself at once; apparent destruction by fire is the non-arising of a similar series.
Things are momentary, but impermanence is a real characteristic acting on each dharma.
Some formations endure for a time (Vasumitra).

name: Seeds and the specific transformation of the series

definitions.definition: Latent defilements, 'possession' and karmic potential are seeds — capacities in the psycho-physical series that mature through its specific transformation, as rice from rice or red pulp from a lac-dyed citron flower.

relations.note: Yogācāra reworks the seeds as stored in the ālaya (historical relation; see borrowings).

definitions.definition: Only the sūtras are authoritative; the Abhidharma treatises are works of named disciples.

name: The Abhidharma as the word of the Buddha

definitions.definition: The Buddha taught the Abhidharma in scattered form; Kātyāyanīputra and others gathered it, as Dharmatrāta gathered the Udāna verses.
Not the Buddha's word; the Abhidharma basket consists of sūtras that teach dharma characteristics.
The Pali tradition holds the seven Abhidhamma books to be buddhavacana (the Kathāvatthu being set out by Moggaliputta Tissa on the Buddha's outline).

name: The seven books of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma

definitions.definition: The Jñānaprasthāna ('body') and six 'feet' — Prakaraṇapāda, Vijñānakāya, Dharmaskandha, Prajñaptiśāstra, Dhātukāya, Saṅgītiparyāya — with authors as listed by Yaśomitra.

relations.note: The Theravāda also has seven books; only partial correspondences (Dharmaskandha ~ Vibhaṅga; Dhātukāya ~ Dhātukathā).

definitions.definition: Between death and birth a being with the form of its coming existence travels to its place of birth, drawn by desire; it feeds on smells.
Accepted (Kv 8.2 commentary).
Denied (Vasumitra).
Denied (Vasumitra).
Denied (Kathāvatthu 8.2).

relations.note: The Tibetan bar do teachings build on the Abhidharma intermediate existence (historical relation).

definitions.definition: Momentary (in one moment), prolonged (over many lives), connected (causally linked), and 'of states' (twelve states of the five aggregates over three lives) — the last is the Vaibhāṣika reading.

name: Dependent origination

definitions.definition: Twelve limbs in three sections over three lives: defilement, karma, ground; a beginningless wheel.

notes: U38 contribution to a shared concept (U36 owns the sutta account).

name: The five aggregates

definitions.definition: The conditioned dharmas grouped as matter, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness; feeling and perception are separated from the other mental factors because they are the roots of dispute and saṃsāra.
Each aggregate is not self (Mahāvastu's version of the second sermon).
The basis on which the person is designated, neither identical with it nor different.

notes: U38 contribution to a shared concept.

name: The four noble truths

definitions.definition: Taught in the order of realization; all that has outflows is suffering; realized in sixteen moments.
Taught at Ṛṣivadana with the two extremes and three turnings.

notes: U38 contribution to a shared concept.

name: Karma as volition and what volition produces

definitions.definition: Karma is volition (mental) and the bodily and vocal action it produces, manifest and unmanifest; fourfold as black, white, black-white and neither.
Mental karma includes covetousness, malice and wrong view.
Bodily and vocal karma are volitions; their results come through the transformed series.

name: The eight kinds of prātimokṣa discipline

definitions.definition: Monk, nun, probationer, male and female novice, male and female lay follower, and the fast-day keeper; four in substance; abstaining from 5, 8, 10 or all things to be avoided.

name: The prātimokṣa rule counts of the Vinayas

definitions.definition: 250 bhikṣu rules, 348 bhikṣuṇī rules.
227 bhikkhu rules (311 bhikkhunī).
218 bhikṣu rules (moderate confidence).
251 bhikṣu rules (low confidence).
263 bhikṣu rules (low confidence).
258 in the Sanskrit prātimokṣa; the Tibetan tradition speaks of 253 vows (low confidence).

notes: Class structure is common to all Vinayas; totals differ mainly in the śaikṣa rules. Only the Dharmaguptaka and Theravāda totals are given with confidence.

definitions.definition: The Dharmaguptaka bhikṣuṇī lineage survives in China, Korea, Vietnam and Taiwan.
Requires dual ordination by bhikṣuṇīs and bhikṣus; the bhikṣuṇī lineage was not transmitted to Tibet.
The bhikkhunī order died out; its revival is disputed (recent).

Three Mūlasarvāstivāda lines: the 'lower Vinaya' from Śāntarakṣita preserved by Lachen Gongpa Rabsal in Amdo; the 'upper Vinaya' from western Tibet; and the lineage of the Kashmiri paṇḍita Śākyaśrībhadra (1204).

name: The six kinds of arhat and falling back

definitions.definition: Liable to fall, able to end life at will, guarding, stable, able to perfect the faculties, unshakeable; five can fall back from what they have obtained.
No falling back from arhatship.
An arahant does not fall away (Kv 1.2).

name: The noble persons in the Abhidharma

definitions.definition: Candidates and fruits of the four stages, distinguished by faculties (follower through faith / through dharma; resolved through faith / attained through view), with subtypes (seven-times, family-to-family, single-interval; five and more kinds of non-returner; body-witness; the six arhats).

name: The four roots of good conducive to penetration

definitions.definition: Heat, summits, acceptance, highest worldly dharmas — worldly cultivation of the sixteen aspects of the four truths before the path of seeing.

relations.note: Mahāyāna places them as the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) of the five paths.

name: Realization of the truths in sixteen moments

definitions.definition: Acceptance and knowledge of dharma and of subsequent knowledge for each truth; fifteen moments are the path of seeing, the sixteenth begins the fruit.
Realization of the truths in one moment is ascribed to the Mahāsāṃghika side in the doxographies (low confidence).
Conventional knowledge, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation and path, of others' minds, of destruction and of non-arising.

Four applications of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven limbs of awakening, eightfold path — ten dharmas in substance, prominent in turn at successive stages.

name: The three concentrations / doors of liberation

definitions.definition: Emptiness, wishless and signless concentrations; pure, they are the three doors of liberation.

name: The six superknowledges and three knowledges

definitions.definition: Magical power, divine ear, others' minds, former lives, death and rebirth, destruction of outflows; three are 'knowledges'; instruction is the highest wonder; power arises from cultivation, birth, spells, herbs or karma.

name: The two aspects of the true Dharma and its decline

definitions.definition: The true Dharma is scripture and realization, upheld by those who teach and practise; since the Teacher has passed, the teaching is at its last breath and seekers must not be heedless.
Categorical, distinguishing, by counter-question, by setting aside.

Three realms; five destinies; the receptacle world on circles of wind, water and gold, with Meru, seven golden ranges, four continents and the iron ring; eight hot and eight cold hells; heavens up to the form realm; world systems grouped in thousands up to the trichiliocosm.

name: The cycle of aeons in the Abhidharmakośa

definitions.definition: A great aeon of eighty intermediate aeons in four periods (formation, duration, destruction, emptiness); human lifespan rises and falls between 80,000 and ten years; decline through craving and bad action; destruction by fire, water and wind.

name: The bodhisattva career in the Sarvāstivāda

definitions.definition: Three incalculable aeons (ending under Ratnaśikhin, Dīpaṅkara, Vipaśyin) and a hundred aeons of karma producing the thirty-two marks; perfections fulfilled as examples show; awakening in thirty-four moments.
Four conducts and ten grounds (Mahāvastu).

name: The Buddha's body and qualities in the Sarvāstivāda

definitions.definition: Refuge in the Buddha is refuge in the non-learner's dharmas that make a Buddha, not in his body; all Buddhas are equal in accumulation, dharma-body and benefit to the world, not in lifespan, caste or stature; the eighteen exclusive qualities.

relations.note: The Lokottaravāda holds the Buddha's bodily life itself to be supramundane.

name: The eighteen exclusive qualities of a Buddha

definitions.definition: Ten powers, four confidences, three applications of mindfulness, great compassion.
Everything about the Buddhas is beyond the world: conduct, merit, postures, body, robes, food, even the fleshly eye.
Tathāgatas are supramundane and without outflows; their body, power and lifespan are limitless; they never sleep and are always in concentration (Vasumitra).
Rejects that the Buddha did not live in the human world (Kv 18.1).
The Buddhas outwardly follow worldly conventions — washing, eating, medicine, ageing — for the sake of beings, without being subject to them.

name: The ten grounds of the Mahāvastu

definitions.definition: Durārohā, Baddhamānā, Puṣpamaṇḍitā, Rucirā, Cittavistarā, Rūpavatī, Durjayā, Janmanideśa, Yauvarājya, Abhiṣeka.

relations.note: The Daśabhūmika's ten grounds (Pramuditā …) have different names and contents; any historical link is a scholarly hypothesis.

definitions.definition: The nature of mind is originally pure, defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
Attributed to the Vibhajyavādins in the Vibhāṣā.
Rejected: a defiled mind is not by nature pure.
A root consciousness underlying the six, reported by Asaṅga as the Mahāsāṃghika precursor of the storehouse consciousness.

relations.note: Asaṅga's Yogācāra identification; not attested in surviving Mahāsāṃghika texts.

definitions.definition: A real person, neither the same as nor different from the aggregates, designated in dependence on them as fire on fuel; inexpressible; the bearer of the burden; that which transmigrates.
No self: only aggregates conditioned by defilement and karma go on like a flame.
The person is a designation of the series; no liberation for those who imagine a self as a separate entity.
The person is not found as a real and ultimate fact.

relations.note: The Pudgalavādins held their person compatible with the Buddha's denial of a self; their opponents did not.

name: The five kinds of knowables (Vātsīputrīya)

definitions.definition: Past, future, present, unconditioned, and the inexpressible (the person).

notes: Known through Vasubandhu's citation (AKBh 9) — an opponent's report.

name: The eighteen schools and their lists

definitions.definition: Vasumitra: nine Mahāsāṃghika and eleven Sthavira groups arising in the second to fourth centuries after the parinirvāṇa.
Dīpavaṃsa/Mahāvaṃsa: eighteen (twelve Theravāda-derived, six Mahāsaṅgītika-derived) plus six later.
Vinītadeva/Tibetan tradition: eighteen in four groups — Sarvāstivāda, Mahāsāṃghika, Saṃmitīya, Sthavira.
Bhavya records a list according to the Saṃmitīyas (details not given here).

notes: The number eighteen is traditional; the actual lists differ in names, counts and derivations.

definitions.definition: Yijing and the Tibetan tradition: Mahāsāṃghika, Sthavira, (Mūla)sarvāstivāda, Saṃmitīya.

name: The first schism: Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika

definitions.definition: After the Vesālī council the defeated Vajjiputtakas formed the Mahāsaṅgītika (Dīpavaṃsa).
Mahādeva's five points split the order under Aśoka (Vasumitra; hostile Vibhāṣā account).
The elders enlarged the Vinaya; the majority kept the old text (Śāriputraparipṛcchā).
Schism proper (saṅghabheda) is a wheel- or act-schism; its lie is the gravest sin.
Rājagaha (after the parinibbāna), Vesālī (a century later, on the ten points), Pāṭaliputta under Aśoka (Kathāvatthu).
A council under Kaniṣka in Kashmir compiled the Vibhāṣā (Xuanzang).
Ten relaxations of the Vinaya practised by the Vajjiputtakas and judged unallowable at the Second Council.
An arhat may be tempted by others, has non-knowing, has doubt, is instructed by others, and the path arises through an utterance — presented as heresy.
Refuted in Kathāvatthu 2.1–2.6 (commentary: Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas).

name: The four Āgamas (Chinese) as parallels to the Nikāyas

definitions.definition: Dīrghāgama (T1) — 30 sūtras.
Madhyamāgama (T26) — 222 sūtras.
Saṃyuktāgama (T99) — 1362 sūtras (Taishō count); also T100 and T101.
Ekottarikāgama (T125) — 472 sūtras; school affiliation debated.
Pali Dhammapada (26 chapters, 423 verses).
Udānavarga (33 chapters, c. 1000 verses).
Gāndhārī Dharmapada (Khotan manuscript).
Patna Dharmapada (22 chapters, c. 414 verses; affiliation proposed).
A Sahasravarga (Dharmapada chapter of thousands) embedded in the Mahāvastu.

Birch-bark scrolls in Gāndhārī (Kharoṣṭhī) from the 1st c. BCE–3rd c. CE, the oldest Buddhist manuscripts: sūtras, verses, Abhidharma, commentaries, avadānas; the British Library scrolls were found in a pot dedicated to the Dharmaguptakas.
